Apple Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis and is one of the most destructive diseases of apple worldwide. It affects leaves, fruit, and twigs, reducing both yield and fruit marketability.
Apple Apple_scab.symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown velvety spots on leaves and fruit. Lesions on fruit become corky and cracked. Severe leaf infection causes premature defoliation.
Apple Apple_scab.causes: Venturia inaequalis overwintering in fallen leaves, warm humid weather (16–25°C), prolonged leaf wetness, and susceptible cultivars.
Apple Apple_scab.prevention: Plant resistant varieties, remove and destroy fallen leaves, prune for airflow, avoid overhead irrigation, and apply dormant copper sprays.
Apple Apple_scab.organic: Sulfur or lime-sulfur sprays, potassium bicarbonate, neem oil, and compost tea to strengthen plant immunity.
Apple Apple_scab.chemical: Captan, myclobutanil, or difenoconazole fungicides applied at green tip through petal fall per local extension schedules.
Apple Apple_scab.fertilizers: Balanced NPK based on soil test; avoid excess nitrogen which promotes susceptible tender growth.
Apple Apple_scab.precautions: Rotate fungicide modes of action to prevent resistance. Do not harvest within pre-harvest intervals on labels.

Apple Black_rot.description: Black rot is a fungal disease caused by Botryosphaeria obtusa that causes fruit rot, leaf spots (frog-eye leaf spot), and canker on apple trees.
Apple Black_rot.symptoms: Purple-bordered brown leaf spots with tan centers (frog-eye). Fruit develops firm brown lesions that expand into concentric rings and mummify.
Apple Black_rot.causes: Fungal spores from mummified fruit and cankers, warm wet conditions, wounding, and stress from drought or frost.
Apple Black_rot.prevention: Remove mummified fruit and dead wood, maintain tree vigor, avoid fruit injury, and sanitize pruning tools.
Apple Black_rot.organic: Copper fungicides, Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicides, and proper orchard sanitation.
Apple Black_rot.chemical: Thiophanate-methyl or captan during bloom and pre-harvest as recommended by extension services.
Apple Black_rot.fertilizers: Adequate potassium and calcium to strengthen cell walls; soil test before applying nitrogen.
Apple Black_rot.precautions: Prune out cankers during dry weather. Burn or bury infected debris away from the orchard.

Apple Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust requires two hosts—apple and eastern red cedar (Juniperus)—to complete its life cycle. Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae causes bright orange leaf lesions on apple.
Apple Cedar_apple_rust.symptoms: Yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surface; tube-like orange structures (aecia) on leaf undersides. Fruit may show similar lesions.
Apple Cedar_apple_rust.causes: Gymnosporangium spores from nearby juniper/cedar trees during spring rains and moderate temperatures.
Apple Cedar_apple_rust.prevention: Remove juniper hosts within 300 m if feasible, plant resistant apple cultivars, and apply protective fungicides at pink bud stage.
Apple Cedar_apple_rust.organic: Sulfur sprays beginning at pink bud; increase distance from cedar/juniper plantings.
Apple Cedar_apple_rust.chemical: Myclobutanil, propiconazole, or trifloxystrobin from pink through second cover spray.
Apple Cedar_apple_rust.fertilizers: Maintain balanced nutrition; stressed trees show more severe rust symptoms.
Apple Cedar_apple_rust.precautions: Monitor nearby cedar galls in early spring. Coordinate sprays with weather during spore release periods.

Apple healthy.description: The apple leaf shows no signs of fungal, bacterial, or physiological disease. Continue standard orchard management for sustained productivity.
Apple healthy.symptoms: Uniform green foliage, intact leaf margins, no spots, lesions, or discoloration.
Apple healthy.causes: N/A — plant tissue is healthy under current growing conditions.
Apple healthy.prevention: Regular scouting, balanced irrigation, dormant pruning, and preventive fungicide programs during high-risk periods.
Apple healthy.organic: Compost mulch, beneficial insect habitat, and seasonal neem or sulfur as preventives.
Apple healthy.chemical: No curative treatment needed; maintain scheduled dormant and pre-bloom protectants if disease pressure exists in the region.
Apple healthy.fertilizers: Annual soil test; apply N-P-K and micronutrients (zinc, boron) per apple orchard recommendations.
Apple healthy.precautions: Monitor weekly during humid seasons. Record spray dates and weather for future planning.

Blueberry healthy.description: Blueberry foliage appears healthy with no mummy berry, anthracnose, or leaf spot symptoms visible.
Blueberry healthy.symptoms: Deep green leaves, normal berry set, no chlorosis or necrotic patches.
Blueberry healthy.prevention: Acidify soil to pH 4.5–5.5, use mulched rows, and prune old canes annually.
Blueberry healthy.organic: Pine bark mulch, elemental sulfur for pH, and fish emulsion for gentle feeding.
Blueberry healthy.chemical: No treatment required unless regional mummy berry pressure warrants dormant fungicides.
Blueberry healthy.fertilizers: Ammonium sulfate or acid-forming fertilizers; avoid nitrate-heavy formulas on low-pH soils.
Blueberry healthy.precautions: Blueberries are sensitive to drought; maintain consistent soil moisture without waterlogging.

Cherry Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on cherry is caused by Podosphaera clandestina, producing white fungal growth on leaves and shoots that reduces photosynthesis and fruit quality.
Cherry Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White powdery patches on leaf surfaces and young shoots. Leaves may curl, distort, and drop prematurely.
Cherry Powdery_mildew.causes: High humidity with dry leaf surfaces, crowded canopies, and moderate temperatures (20–27°C).
Cherry Powdery_mildew.prevention: Prune for sunlight penetration, avoid excessive nitrogen, and plant less susceptible cultivars.
Cherry Powdery_mildew.organic: Potassium bicarbonate, milk spray (1:10 dilution), sulfur, and horticultural oils on young infections.
Cherry Powdery_mildew.chemical: Myclobutanil, trifloxystrobin, or sulfur fungicides at shuck split and post-harvest if needed.
Cherry Powdery_mildew.fertilizers: Moderate nitrogen; excess promotes succulent mildew-susceptible growth.
Cherry Powdery_mildew.precautions: Apply sulfur only below 30°C to avoid phytotoxicity. Alternate fungicide classes.

Cherry healthy.description: Cherry leaves show no powdery mildew, bacterial canker, or leaf spot. Maintain orchard hygiene for continued health.
Cherry healthy.symptoms: Glossy green leaves, no white coating or shot-hole lesions.
Cherry healthy.prevention: Dormant copper, balanced pruning, and bird netting before fruit ripening.
Cherry healthy.organic: Compost tea foliar feeds and kaolin clay for pest deterrence.
Cherry healthy.chemical: Preventive program only if regional disease history exists.
Cherry healthy.fertilizers: Light nitrogen in spring; potassium and phosphorus per soil analysis after harvest.
Cherry healthy.precautions: Avoid wounding trunks during harvest; wounds invite bacterial canker.

Corn Cercospora_leaf_spot.description: Cercospora leaf spot (gray leaf spot) is caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis and C. zeina, producing rectangular lesions that reduce photosynthetic area in maize.
Corn Cercospora_leaf_spot.symptoms: Narrow rectangular tan to gray lesions bounded by leaf veins. Lesions fuse under severe infection causing blighting.
Corn Cercospora_leaf_spot.causes: Corn residue harboring inoculum, warm humid weather, continuous corn cropping, and susceptible hybrids.
Corn Cercospora_leaf_spot.prevention: Rotate with non-host crops, till or manage residue, plant resistant hybrids, and scout from V8 stage.
Corn Cercospora_leaf_spot.organic: Crop rotation (2+ years), residue management, and foliar biologicals containing Bacillus species.
Corn Cercospora_leaf_spot.chemical: Strobilurin or triazole fungicides at VT–R1 if lesion threshold exceeded (e.g., on ear leaf).
Corn Cercospora_leaf_spot.fertilizers: Balanced fertility; adequate potassium improves tolerance. Avoid late excessive nitrogen.
Corn Cercospora_leaf_spot.precautions: Fungicide timing is critical—late applications give minimal yield benefit.

Corn Common_rust.description: Common rust of corn is caused by Puccinia sorghi, forming cinnamon-brown pustules on leaves that can reduce yield in susceptible varieties.
Corn Common_rust.symptoms: Small oval cinnamon-brown pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces. Severe rust causes leaf chlorosis and early senescence.
Corn Common_rust.causes: Urediniospores from southern overwintering regions, cool nights (16–25°C), dew, and susceptible germplasm.
Corn Common_rust.prevention: Plant rust-resistant/tolerant hybrids, scout early, and avoid late-planted fields in high-pressure years.
Corn Common_rust.organic: Resistant varieties are primary control; remove volunteer corn in rotation fields.
Corn Common_rust.chemical: Triazole or strobilurin fungicides if rust reaches ear leaf before tasseling in seed or high-value corn.
Corn Common_rust.fertilizers: Standard corn N program split-applied; ensure sulfur and zinc if deficient per tissue test.
Corn Common_rust.precautions: Common rust rarely warrants treatment on modern tolerant hybrids—confirm severity before spraying.

Corn Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB) is caused by Exserohilum turcicum, producing elongated elliptical lesions that can defoliate upper canopy layers.
Corn Northern_Leaf_Blight.symptoms: Cigar-shaped tan lesions 2–15 cm long with dark borders. Lesions merge under heavy pressure.
Corn Northern_Leaf_Blight.causes: Infected corn residue, warm humid conditions, continuous corn, and susceptible hybrids.
Corn Northern_Leaf_Blight.prevention: Residue management, crop rotation, resistant hybrids with Ht genes, and early scouting.
Corn Northern_Leaf_Blight.organic: Two-year rotation, residue incorporation, and biological fungicides as supplements.
Corn Northern_Leaf_Blight.chemical: Fungicides at VT if lesions appear on third leaf below ear or above on 50% of plants.
Corn Northern_Leaf_Blight.fertilizers: Follow extension N recommendations; potassium aids stalk health post-infection.
Corn Northern_Leaf_Blight.precautions: Northern leaf blight spreads quickly in foggy valleys—monitor weather forecasts.

Corn healthy.description: Maize foliage is free of rust, blight, and leaf spot symptoms. Continue integrated crop management through grain fill.
Corn healthy.symptoms: Dark green leaves without lesions; normal tassel and ear development.
Corn healthy.prevention: Hybrid selection, balanced fertility, timely weed control, and moisture management.
Corn healthy.organic: Cover crops in rotation and compost-based fertility programs.
Corn healthy.chemical: Seed treatment fungicide/insecticide as standard; foliar sprays only if scouting warrants.
Corn healthy.fertilizers: Split N application (planting + side-dress); P and K per soil test.
Corn healthy.precautions: Scout from V6 through R3 for early disease detection.

Grape Black_rot.description: Grape black rot, caused by Guignardia bidwellii, destroys fruit and causes leaf lesions in humid viticulture regions worldwide.
Grape Black_rot.symptoms: Circular tan leaf spots with dark borders; fruit shrivels into hard black mummies. Shoot lesions appear as elliptical tan spots.
Grape Black_rot.causes: Ascospores from mummified berries and overwintered lesions during spring rains 24–27°C.
Grape Black_rot.prevention: Remove mummies, open canopy for airflow, shoot positioning, and protective fungicides from bud break.
Grape Black_rot.organic: Copper, sulfur, and lime-sulfur; strict sanitation of infected clusters.
Grape Black_rot.chemical: Mancozeb, myclobutanil, or captan on 7–14 day intervals during wet spring periods.
Grape Black_rot.fertilizers: Moderate nitrogen; excess vigor creates dense canopy favorable to black rot.
Grape Black_rot.precautions: Eliminate wild grapevines nearby. Time sprays before rainfall events.

Grape Esca.description: Esca is a complex trunk disease of grapevines involving fungi such as Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Fomitiporia mediterranea, causing leaf stripe symptoms and vine decline.
Grape Esca.symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis and necrosis (tiger-stripe leaves), berry speckling, sudden wilting of shoots, and wood decay.
Grape Esca.causes: Fungal colonization through pruning wounds, vine age, stress, and spread via infected tools and rain splash.
Grape Esca.prevention: Prune in dry weather, double-cut larger wounds, delay pruning in cold regions, and remove severely affected vines.
Grape Esca.organic: Trichoderma wound dressings, bio-control on pruning cuts, and balanced vine nutrition.
Grape Esca.chemical: Sodium arsenite (restricted/banned in many regions)—focus on cultural and wound protection; consult local regulations.
Grape Esca.fertilizers: Avoid over-cropping on weakened vines; replenish potassium and magnesium if deficient.
Grape Esca.precautions: Disinfect pruning tools between vines (10% bleach or 70% ethanol). Esca has no reliable curative spray.

Grape___Leaf_blight.description: Grape leaf blight (Isariopsis leaf spot) causes angular brown lesions on leaves, often following injury or stress on grapevines.
Grape___Leaf_blight.symptoms: Brown necrotic lesions often angular in shape, sometimes with yellow halos. Defoliation occurs in severe cases.
Grape___Leaf_blight.causes: Pseudocercosp vitis and related pathogens favored by warm wet weather and leaf damage.
Grape___Leaf_blight.prevention: Canopy management, avoid leaf wounding, and copper protectants during wet periods.
Grape___Leaf_blight.organic: Copper fungicides, removal of heavily infected leaves, and improved air circulation.
Grape___Leaf_blight.chemical: Mancozeb or captan with good canopy penetration during pre-bloom and berry touch sprays.
Grape___Leaf_blight.fertilizers: Balanced vine nutrition; zinc and boron deficiencies increase susceptibility to leaf disorders.
Grape___Leaf_blight.precautions: Do not confuse with downy mildew—confirm diagnosis before altering spray program.

Grape___healthy.description: Grapevine leaves and clusters show no black rot, downy mildew, or esca stripe symptoms.
Grape___healthy.symptoms: Uniform green canopy, intact berries, no necrotic leaf patterns.
Grape___healthy.prevention: Standard IPM spray program, canopy hedging, and balanced crop load.
Grape___healthy.organic: Sulfur and copper rotation, compost under-vine, and beneficial mite preservation.
Grape___healthy.chemical: Maintain preventive schedule only during disease-conducive weather.
Grape___healthy.fertilizers: Petiole analysis at bloom; adjust N, K, and micronutrients accordingly.
Grape___healthy.precautions: Record phenology stages for accurate spray timing each season.

Orange___Haunglongbing.description: Huanglongbing (HLB), or citrus greening, is a devastating bacterial disease transmitted by Asian citrus psyllid. Infected trees decline and produce misshapen, bitter fruit.
Orange___Haunglongbing.symptoms: Blotchy mottle on leaves, yellow shoots, lopsided bitter fruit with aborted seeds, and twig dieback.
Orange___Haunglongbing.causes: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus transmitted by Diaphorina citri psyllid; grafting with infected budwood.
Orange___Haunglongbing.prevention: Use certified disease-free nursery trees, control psyllids, remove HLB-positive trees, and enforce quarantine zones.
Orange___Haunglongbing.organic: Reflective mulches, kaolin clay, beneficial releases, and nutritional therapies to slow decline.
Orange___Haunglongbing.chemical: Systemic insecticides (imidacloprid, thiamethoxam) for psyllid control; antibiotics where legally permitted under strict programs.
Orange___Haunglongbing.fertilizers: Enhanced nutrition programs (N, K, Ca, Mg, Zn, Mn, Fe, B) via soil and foliar feeds to mitigate symptoms.
Orange___Haunglongbing.precautions: There is no cure for HLB—early detection and tree removal limit spread. Report suspect trees to agricultural authorities.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Peach bacterial spot, caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, affects leaves, fruit, and twigs, causing defoliation and fruit pitting.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small angular water-soaked leaf spots turning purple-brown; fruit pitting and cracking; twig cankers on susceptible cultivars.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.causes: Bacteria overwintering in buds and twigs, rain splash, wind, and warm humid spring weather.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Plant resistant cultivars, avoid overhead irrigation, apply copper at dormant and shuck-split stages.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.organic: Copper hydroxide, Bacillus-based bactericides, and orchard sanitation.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.chemical: Copper plus oxytetracycline (where labeled) during extended wet periods in spring.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.fertilizers: Avoid excessive nitrogen; adequate potassium and calcium improve fruit skin integrity.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.precautions: Copper can russet fruit—follow rates carefully near harvest. Alternate management tactics yearly.

Peach___healthy.description: Peach foliage and fruit show no bacterial spot, leaf curl, or brown rot symptoms.
Peach___healthy.symptoms: Healthy green leaves, smooth fruit skin, normal shoot extension.
Peach___healthy.prevention: Dormant copper, proper thinning, and brown rot program near harvest.
Peach___healthy.organic: Compost mulch and sulfur for brown rot prevention on fruit.
Peach___healthy.chemical: Standard dormant and pre-harvest fungicide program per local peach guide.
Peach___healthy.fertilizers: N applied early season; P and K per soil test after leaf fall analysis.
Peach___healthy.precautions: Prune annually to maintain open center and reduce leaf wetness duration.

Pepper___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot on pepper is caused by Xanthomonas euvesicatoria, producing leaf and fruit lesions that reduce marketable yield in warm humid climates.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves turning brown; raised scabby lesions on fruit; defoliation under severe pressure.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.causes: Contaminated seed, infected transplants, splashing rain, high humidity, and warm temperatures (24–30°C).
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.prevention: Use certified seed, hot-water seed treatment, crop rotation (2+ years), drip irrigation, and resistant varieties.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.organic: Copper sprays, streptomycin where permitted, and strict transplant inspection.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.chemical: Copper-mancozeb combinations and actigard (plant activator) per label during transplant establishment.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.fertilizers: Balanced fertigation; excess nitrogen increases susceptibility.
Pepper___Bacterial_spot.precautions: Avoid working fields when foliage is wet. Destroy crop residue after final harvest.

Pepper___healthy.description: Pepper plants show no bacterial spot, anthracnose, or viral mosaic symptoms.
Pepper___healthy.symptoms: Dark green leaves, uniform fruit coloration, no leaf drop.
Pepper___healthy.prevention: Sanitize stakes and tools, use virus-free transplants, and monitor aphid vectors.
Pepper___healthy.organic: Neem for aphid suppression and reflective mulch in virus-prone areas.
Pepper___healthy.chemical: Preventive copper at transplant if bacterial spot history exists on farm.
Pepper___healthy.fertilizers: Calcium nitrate during fruit set to prevent blossom-end rot; K during fruit sizing.
Pepper___healthy.precautions: Do not smoke near peppers (tobacco mosaic virus transmission on hands).

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight of potato, caused by Alternaria solani, produces concentric ring lesions on lower leaves and can reduce tuber yield if unmanaged.
Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown lesions with target-board concentric rings on older leaves. Yellow halo and defoliation progress upward.
Potato___Early_blight.causes: Alternaria spores in soil and debris, plant stress, nitrogen deficiency, warm alternating wet/dry periods.
Potato___Early_blight.prevention: Rotate crops, maintain fertility, hill soil to protect tubers, and irrigate consistently.
Potato___Early_blight.organic: Copper, Bacillus subtilis, remove lower infected leaves, and compost teas.
Potato___Early_blight.chemical: Chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin on 7–10 day intervals when conditions favor disease.
Potato___Early_blight.fertilizers: Adequate N and K; foliar manganese and zinc if deficient to reduce stress.
Potato___Early_blight.precautions: Begin fungicide program before lesions reach upper canopy. Calibrate sprayer for full coverage.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is the same pathogen responsible for the Irish potato famine. It destroys foliage and tubers rapidly in cool wet weather.
Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked gray-green leaf lesions turning brown-black; white sporulation on undersides in humidity; tuber reddish-brown rot.
Potato___Late_blight.causes: Phytophthora infestans spores spread by wind and rain, cool nights (10–15°C), high humidity, and infected seed tubers.
Potato___Late_blight.prevention: Certified seed, destroy cull piles, hilling, scout daily in risky weather, and regional alert networks.
Potato___Late_blight.organic: Copper fungicides, remove infected plants immediately, and avoid overhead irrigation.
Potato___Late_blight.chemical: Mandipropamid, fluopicolide, or cymoxanil + mancozeb on tight intervals during epidemics.
Potato___Late_blight.fertilizers: Balanced nutrition; avoid excess N late season which delays maturity and extends susceptibility.
Potato___Late_blight.precautions: Late blight is notifiable in many regions—report outbreaks. Do not store infected tubers.

Potato___healthy.description: Potato foliage shows no early or late blight lesions. Continue hilling and tuber bulking management.
Potato___healthy.symptoms: Green vigorous canopy without necrotic patches or sporulation.
Potato___healthy.prevention: Certified seed, rotation, blight forecasting, and preventive fungicides in high-risk zones.
Potato___healthy.organic: Compost and cover crops in rotation; copper only if organic certification allows.
Potato___healthy.chemical: Follow regional blight spray calendar from emergence through senescence.
Potato___healthy.fertilizers: Split N application; P at planting; K critical for tuber quality and disease tolerance.
Potato___healthy.precautions: Monitor met forecasts for Smith Periods or similar blight risk models.

Raspberry___healthy.description: Raspberry canes and leaves appear free of anthracnose, spur blight, and rust.
Raspberry___healthy.symptoms: Healthy compound leaves, strong primocane growth, clean fruit.
Raspberry___healthy.prevention: Annual cane thinning, trellising, weed control, and dormant lime-sulfur where labeled.
Raspberry___healthy.organic: Compost mulch, proper spacing, and removal of floricanes after harvest.
Raspberry___healthy.chemical: Dormant fungicide if gray mold or spur blight occurred previous season.
Raspberry___healthy.fertilizers: Moderate N in spring; avoid late-season N that reduces winter hardiness.
Raspberry___healthy.precautions: Ensure good drainage—Phytophthora root rot mimics nutrient stress.

Soybean___healthy.description: Soybean plants show no bacterial blight, frogeye leaf spot, or rust symptoms.
Soybean___healthy.symptoms: Trifoliate leaves uniformly green, normal pod set, no leaf chlorosis patterns.
Soybean___healthy.prevention: Resistant varieties, seed treatment, crop rotation, and scouting from R1.
Soybean___healthy.organic: Inoculate with Bradyrhizobium, cover crop rotation, and timely weed management.
Soybean___healthy.chemical: Foliar fungicide only if frogeye or rust thresholds met before R3.
Soybean___healthy.fertilizers: Inoculation supplies N; ensure adequate P, K, and molybdenum on acidic soils.
Soybean___healthy.precautions: Identify herbicide drift vs. disease—pattern follows sprayer swaths.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on squash is caused by Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum, coating leaves with white mycelium and reducing fruit size.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.symptoms: White powdery fungal growth on leaf upper surfaces. Leaves turn yellow, brown, and die. Fruit sunburns due to defoliation.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.causes: Warm days, cool nights, dense foliage, and mid-to-late season inoculum buildup.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.prevention: Plant resistant varieties, space plants widely, and apply sulfur or oil early at first sign.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.organic: Potassium bicarbonate, milk spray, sulfur, and removal of oldest infected leaves.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.chemical: Quinoxyfen, triflumizole, or azoxystrobin when 1 lesion per 45 leaves threshold reached.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.fertilizers: Avoid late heavy nitrogen; maintain potassium for fruit quality.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.precautions: Sulfur damages plants above 32°C. Alternate modes of action to manage resistance.

Strawberry Leaf_scorch.description: Strawberry leaf scorch is caused by Diplocarpon earlianum, producing purple spots that coalesce and cause leaf burn appearance.
Strawberry Leaf_scorch.symptoms: Small purple spots on upper leaf surface without distinct centers. Spots merge; leaves appear scorched. Petiole lesions possible.
Strawberry Leaf_scorch.causes: Fungal spores in infected leaves and debris, splashing water, warm humid weather during fruiting.
Strawberry Leaf_scorch.prevention: Use clean transplants, straw mulch, renovation after harvest, and resistant cultivars where available.
Strawberry Leaf_scorch.organic: Copper, neem, remove infected leaves, and ensure row airflow.
Strawberry Leaf_scorch.chemical: Captan or thiram during bloom and post-harvest renovation sprays.
Strawberry Leaf_scorch.fertilizers: Balanced bed nutrition before planting; foliar calcium during fruiting.
Strawberry Leaf_scorch.precautions: Do not apply captan during peak bee activity—spray evenings if needed.

Strawberry___healthy.description: Strawberry leaves and fruit show no leaf scorch, gray mold, or angular leaf spot.
Strawberry___healthy.symptoms: Green trifoliate leaves, clean berries, vigorous runners.
Strawberry___healthy.prevention: Mulch, renovation, rotate beds every 3–4 years, and fungicide at bloom if wet.
Strawberry___healthy.organic: Straw mulch, compost, and Bacillus for botrytis suppression.
Strawberry___healthy.chemical: Preventive fungicide during bloom only if gray mold pressure is high.
Strawberry___healthy.fertilizers: Split N through season; avoid excess late N before dormancy.
Strawberry___healthy.precautions: Renovate beds promptly after harvest to regenerate healthy foliage.

Tomato Bacterial_spot.description: Tomato bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas species, causing leaf spotting, defoliation, and fruit lesions that reduce yield and quality.
Tomato Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small dark brown leaf spots with yellow halos; raised scabby fruit spots; severe defoliation in wet seasons.
Tomato Bacterial_spot.causes: Contaminated seed/transplants, rain splash, high humidity, and warm temperatures.
Tomato Bacterial_spot.prevention: Certified transplants, crop rotation, drip irrigation, stake plants, and copper at transplant.
Tomato Bacterial_spot.organic: Copper bactericides, Actinovate, and strict sanitation between fields.
Tomato Bacterial_spot.chemical: Copper + mancozeb rotations; acibenzolar-S-methyl plant defense activator.
Tomato Bacterial_spot.fertilizers: Balanced fertigation; calcium foliar during fruit development.
Tomato Bacterial_spot.precautions: Avoid overhead irrigation. Remove volunteer tomatoes and nightshades.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Tomato early blight (Alternaria solani) affects leaves, stems, and fruit, typically starting on lower foliage and progressing upward.
Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Brown lesions with concentric rings on lower leaves; stem cankers; fruit lesions near stem attachment.
Tomato___Early_blight.causes: Alternaria in crop debris, plant stress, alternating moisture, and dense planting.
Tomato___Early_blight.prevention: Mulch soil, prune lower leaves, rotate 2+ years, and stake/cage for airflow.
Tomato___Early_blight.organic: Copper, Bacillus subtilis, remove infected lower leaves, and compost tea.
Tomato___Early_blight.chemical: Chlorothalonil, azoxystrobin, or difenoconazole starting at first fruit set if lesions appear.
Tomato___Early_blight.fertilizers: Consistent moisture and potassium; avoid N stress or excess.
Tomato___Early_blight.precautions: Sanitize stakes yearly. Do not compost severely infected vines.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Tomato late blight (Phytophthora infestans) spreads explosively in cool wet weather, destroying foliage and fruit within days.
Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Large irregular brown leaf patches; white fuzzy sporulation on undersides; firm brown fruit lesions.
Tomato___Late_blight.causes: Airborne Phytophthora spores, infected transplants, cool humid nights, and proximity to infected potatoes.
Tomato___Late_blight.prevention: Use resistant varieties where available, certified plants, spacing, and regional blight alerts.
Tomato___Late_blight.organic: Copper protectants, destroy infected plants in sealed bags, avoid overhead water.
Tomato___Late_blight.chemical: Mandipropamid, fluopicolide, or chlorothalonil + cymoxanil during high-risk periods.
Tomato___Late_blight.fertilizers: Maintain plant vigor without excessive late N; calcium for fruit firmness.
Tomato___Late_blight.precautions: Late blight spreads rapidly—act within 24 hours of confirmation. Report to local extension.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Tomato leaf mold (Passalora fulva) is common in greenhouses and high tunnels, causing yellowing and mold growth on leaf undersides.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on upper leaf surface; olive-green to gray velvety mold on undersides. Defoliation in humid houses.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.causes: High humidity (>85%), poor ventilation, susceptible varieties, and spores on debris and structures.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.prevention: Vent heat and humidity, resistant cultivars, drip irrigation, and sanitize greenhouse between crops.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.organic: Improve airflow, sulfur vaporizers (greenhouse), and remove lower infected leaves.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.chemical: Chlorothalonil, difenoconazole, or fluxapyroxad in protected culture.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.fertilizers: Avoid excess N in high humidity; maintain EC in hydroponics within optimal range.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.precautions: Leaf mold rarely occurs in open field with good airflow—adjust environment before heavy spraying.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot (Septoria lycopersici) causes numerous small circular spots on tomato leaves, leading to defoliation from the bottom up.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Small circular gray spots with dark borders and tiny black pycnidia in centers. Lower leaves yellow and drop first.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.causes: Fungal spores splashed from soil, wet foliage, warm temperatures, and infected crop residue.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.prevention: Mulch, crop rotation, stake plants, prune lower leaves, and avoid working wet plants.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.organic: Copper, Bacillus, remove infected leaves, and destroy debris at season end.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.chemical: Chlorothalonil or mancozeb on 7–10 day schedule when disease appears.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.fertilizers: Balanced field nutrition; foliar feeds if defoliation stresses fruit fill.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.precautions: Septoria often co-occurs with early blight—use products effective on both if confirmed.

Tomato___Spider_mites.description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) are arachnid pests causing stippling and bronzing of tomato leaves, especially under hot dry conditions.
Tomato___Spider_mites.symptoms: Fine yellow stippling on leaves, webbing on undersides, leaf bronzing and desiccation, reduced fruit size.
Tomato___Spider_mites.causes: Hot dry weather, dust, broad-spectrum insecticide use killing natural enemies, and drought stress.
Tomato___Spider_mites.prevention: Overhead syringing (greenhouse), preserve predatory mites, avoid dusty paths, and maintain adequate irrigation.
Tomato___Spider_mites.organic: Predatory Phytoseiulus persimilis, neem oil, insecticidal soap, and horticultural oil.
Tomato___Spider_mites.chemical: Abamectin, spiromesifen, or bifenazate—rotate modes; avoid pyrethroids which flare mites.
Tomato___Spider_mites.fertilizers: Moderate nitrogen—excess promotes tender foliage favored by mites. Ensure adequate water.
Tomato___Spider_mites.precautions: Mites develop resistance quickly—never repeat same miticide class consecutively.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot on tomato is caused by Corynespora cassiicola, producing circular lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit in warm humid climates.
Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Brown circular lesions with concentric rings and yellow halos on leaves. Fruit spots with sunken centers.
Tomato___Target_Spot.causes: Corynespora spores in debris, high humidity, warm temperatures (25–30°C), and dense canopies.
Tomato___Target_Spot.prevention: Crop rotation, ventilation in tunnels, resistant varieties where available, and fungicide before canopy closure.
Tomato___Target_Spot.organic: Copper, Bacillus, canopy pruning, and residue destruction.
Tomato___Target_Spot.chemical: Azoxystrobin, difenoconazole, or chlorothalonil when lesions first detected.
Tomato___Target_Spot.fertilizers: Balanced nutrition; silicon supplements may strengthen epidermal tissue.
Tomato___Target_Spot.precautions: Target spot mimics early blight—microscopic ID confirms pathogen before program changes.

Tomato___Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) is transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci), causing severe stunting and yield loss in tropical and subtropical production.
Tomato___Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Upward leaf curling, yellow leaf margins, stunted growth, flower drop, and few or no marketable fruit.
Tomato___Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.causes: TYLCV transmitted persistently by whiteflies; infected transplants and weed hosts.
Tomato___Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.prevention: TYLCV-resistant varieties, whitefly-proof netting, yellow sticky traps, and rogue infected plants early.
Tomato___Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.organic: Reflective mulches, neem oil, Encarsia parasitoid releases, and strict weed control.
Tomato___Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.chemical: Imidacloprid or dinotefuran at transplant; spiromesifen for nymphs—viricides do not exist.
Tomato___Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.fertilizers: Support mildly infected plants with balanced fertigation; severe plants should be removed.
Tomato___Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.precautions: Uproot and bag infected plants immediately. Control whiteflies before virus spreads.

Tomato___Mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) causes mottling, leaf distortion, and reduced fruit quality. It spreads mechanically on hands, tools, and tobacco products.
Tomato___Mosaic_virus.symptoms: Light and dark green mottle on leaves, fern-leaf distortion, stunting, brown streaks on stems, uneven fruit ripening.
Tomato___Mosaic_virus.causes: Mechanical transmission, infected seed, contaminated tools, and handling after smoking tobacco.
Tomato___Mosaic_virus.prevention: Use TMV-resistant varieties, sanitize tools with 10% bleach, wash hands, and avoid tobacco near crops.
Tomato___Mosaic_virus.organic: Remove infected plants; milk dip for hands/tools has limited benefit—sanitation is key.
Tomato___Mosaic_virus.chemical: No chemical cures viruses—focus on prevention and vector/mechanical control.
Tomato___Mosaic_virus.fertilizers: Maintain nutrition on mildly affected plants; remove severely stunted plants to protect the block.
Tomato___Mosaic_virus.precautions: Designate clean workers for young plant handling. Disinfect pruning tools between plants.

Tomato___healthy.description: Tomato plants show no bacterial, fungal, viral, or mite damage. Continue standard IPM through harvest.
Tomato___healthy.symptoms: Deep green leaves, normal flowering, fruit set without deformities.
Tomato___healthy.prevention: Sanitation, staking, mulching, whitefly monitoring, and balanced irrigation.
Tomato___healthy.organic: Compost, neem for preventive pest suppression, and beneficial insect habitat.
Tomato___healthy.chemical: Only treat when scouting thresholds exceeded—avoid calendar sprays on healthy plants.
Tomato___healthy.fertilizers: Split N-P-K fertigation; calcium and boron during flowering and fruit enlargement.
Tomato___healthy.precautions: Scout twice weekly in peak season. Record varieties and dates for rotation planning.
